post.caption: This opal turns clear in water. It is a hydrophane opal, which soaks up water like a sponge. Much of the opal from Ethiopia's Welo Province is hydrophane, and the main find came in 2008, near the town of Wegel Tena. A soaked stone can gain up to 15 percent in weight, and drying back to its usual look can take days. Its play of color is often vivid, like Australian opal, but Ethiopian opal formed in volcanic rock, unlike Australia's sedimentary opal. Many jewelers say pendants and earrings suit it better than rings. Treat it like a pearl, and never soak it.
